rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The meaning of mercy was explained earlier in al-Fātiḥa.
rows.anchor: وتقدم معنى الرحمة في سورة الفاتحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Putting raʾūf before raḥīm makes raḥīm the verse ending, fitting the sūrah's cadence; the sounds in raʾūf also make a more difficult pause.
rows.anchor: وتقديم ( رءوف ) ليقع لفظ رحيم فاصلة فيكون أنسب بفواصل هذه السورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Placing “by the people” before the two predicates foregrounds God's care so they will give thanks, while also serving the cadence.
rows.anchor: وتقديم { بالناس } على متعلقه وهو { رءوف رحيم } للتنبيه على عنايته بهم

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read لرءوف with a wāw after the hamza.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور ( لرءوف ) بواو ساكنة بعد الهمزة

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو وحمزة والكسائي ويعقوب وخلف
rows.claim: These readers omit the wāw and put ḍamma on the hamza, following a non-regular dialect form.
rows.anchor: وقرأه أبو عمرو وحمزة والكسائي ويعقوب وخلف بدون واو مع ضم الهمزة بوزن عضد وهو لغة على غير قياس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opening with patience prepares believers for a major deed and severe trial, namely jihad, perhaps preparing them for the great Battle of Badr.
rows.anchor: وفي افتتاح هذا الخطاب بالاستعانة بالصبر إيذان بأنه سيعقب بالندب إلى عمل عظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The qibla changed in Rajab or Shaʿbān of year two; Buwāṭ, al-ʿUshayra, and the first Badr expedition followed in Rabīʿ and Jumādā without fighting, and the major Badr came in Ramadan about two months later.
rows.anchor: وكانت غزوة بواط والعشيرة وبدر الأولى في ربيع وجمادى من السنة الثانية ولم يكن فيهما قتال

rows.speaker: البراء بن عازب
rows.claim: A narrator's report that people had been killed before the qibla change was, Ibn ʿĀshūr says, a mistaken inference by one transmitter from al-Barāʾ.
rows.anchor: أن ما وقع في حديث البراء بن عازب من قول الراوي أن ناسا قتلوا قبل تحويل القبلة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In al-Tirmidhī's report, after the Prophet turned toward the Kaaba, people asked about their brothers who had died while praying toward Jerusalem; the report does not say they were killed.
rows.anchor: والأصح ما في حديث الترمذي عن ابن عباس قال ( لما وجه النبي إلى الكعبة قالوا يا رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage prepares Muslims to endure the hardships of war and makes martyrdom dear to them.
rows.anchor: فالوجه في تفسير هذه الآية أنها تهيئة للمسلمين للصبر على شدائد الحرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The present-tense wording “who is killed” points to a future event: the believers killed at Badr soon after this verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: ولذلك وقع التعبير بالمضارع في قوله : { لمن يقتل في سبيل الله المشعر بأنه أمر مستقبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike the address to the Israelites, this verse does not say patience is hard except for the humble, implying Muslims were enabled to do what was hard for others and are those humble people.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا إيماء إلى أن المسلمين قد يسر لهم ما يصعب على غيرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The added promise that God is with the patient assures Muslims they will obey this command and join the ranks of the patient.
rows.anchor: فبشرهم بأنهم ممن يمتثل هذا الأمر ويعد لذلك في زمرة الصابرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “God is with the patient” concludes the command by way of justification: be patient so God will be with you, since He is with the patient.
rows.anchor: وقوله { إن الله مع الصابرين } تذييل في معنى التعليل أي اصبروا ليكون الله معكم لأنه مع الصابرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition on calling those killed in God's path dead follows the command to endure war, since death is the hardest trial of patience.
rows.anchor: عطف النهي على الأمر قبله لمناسبة التعرض للغزو مما يتوقع معه القتل في سبيل الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The martyr's honor after death turns patience into gratitude, while the family can be assured of the martyr's everlasting life.
rows.anchor: نبه مع ذلك على أن هذا الصبر ينقلب شكرا عندما يرى الشهيد كرامته بعد الشهادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse completes the assurance that God will not let believers' faith go to waste: the earlier martyrs' merit is not diminished.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن هذا تكميل لقوله : { وما كان الله ليضيع إيمانكم } ( البقرة : 143 )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Do not say” forbids the belief behind the statement, because people speak only what they believe.
rows.anchor: فقوله : { ولا تقولوا } نهي عن القول الناشىء عن اعتقاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammatically, “dead” is the predicate of an omitted subject: “do not say, they are dead.”
rows.anchor: وارتفع { أموات } على أنه خبر لمبتدأ محذوف أي لا تقولوا هم أموات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Rather” cancels the forbidden assertion and introduces the standalone assertion “they are alive”; it does not instruct the audience to say they are alive.
rows.anchor: و { بل } للإضراب الإبطالي إبطالا لمضمون المنهي عن قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Martyrs' life is spiritual rather than bodily or material, yet exceeds the ordinary life of souls, which persist and have some awareness while awaiting resurrection.
rows.anchor: للإشارة إلى أنها حياة غير جسمية ولا مادية بل حياة روحية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says martyrs' spirits are placed in green birds that graze on the fruits of Paradise and drink its water; their souls receive a suitable body so bodily senses can mediate pleasure.
rows.anchor: ولذلك ورد في الحديث ( إن أرواح الشهداء تجعل في حواصل طيور خضر ترعى من ثمر الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After mentioning the curse and hell for associating partners with God, the verse says the one they disbelieved in is one God; this supports reading “those who disbelieved” as polytheists, since People of the Book affirm one God.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر ما ينالهم على الشرك من اللعنة والخلود في النار بين أن الذي كفروا به وأشركوا هو إلاه واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural address includes anyone who could hear or read the Qur'an at revelation or later, while its initial target is polytheists who failed to recognize God's oneness.
rows.anchor: والخطاب بكاف الجمع لكل من يتأتى خطابه وقت نزول الآية أو بعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Arabic, ilāh means an object of worship; applying it to idols reflects error about true divinity, since worshipping what can help neither itself nor its worshipper is futile.
rows.anchor: والإلاه في كلام العرب هو المعبود ولذلك تعددت الآلهة عندهم وأطلق لفظ الإلاه على كل صنم عبدوه وهو إطلاق ناشىء عن الضلال في حقيقة الإلاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God the one ilāh is no semantic shift: it confirms that He alone is truly worthy of worship.
rows.anchor: فوصف الإلاه هنا بالواحد لأنه في نفس الأمر هو المعبود بحق فليس إطلاق الإلاه على المعبود بحق نقلا في لغة الإسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an uses the plural “gods” for idols to expose the polytheists' error, as in 46:28; it never uses singular ilāh for an illegitimate deity.
rows.anchor: وما ورد في القرآن من إطلاق جمع الآلهة على أصنامهم فهو في مقام التغليط لزعمهم نحو { فلولا نصرهم الذين اتخذوا من دون الله قربانا آلهة بل ضلوا عنهم وذلك إفكهم وما كانوا يفترون } ( الأحقاف : 28 )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating ilāh between subject and predicate means “your God is one,” while foregrounding divinity and treating the following quality as a settled attribute rather than a new condition.
rows.anchor: والمقصود وإلاهكم واحد لكنه وسط لفظ { إلاه } بين المبتدأ والخبر لتقرير معنى الألوهية في المخبر عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This repeated-name construction is used in eloquent speech; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 2:133 and 25:27 as parallels.
rows.anchor: وهذا استعمال متبع في فصيح الكلام أن يعاد الاسم أو الفعل بعد ذكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite ilāh is generic, establishing the meaning of divinity; unity is already supplied by “one.”
rows.anchor: والتنكير في { إله } للنوعية لأن المقصود منه تقرير معنى الألوهية

rows.speaker: صاحب المفتاح
rows.claim: Al-Sakkākī takes the indefinite ilāh in 6:19 as marking a single individual and treats “one” as an explanation of unity.
rows.anchor: خلافا لصاحب ( المفتاح ) في قوله تعالى : { إنما هو إله واحد } ( الأنعام : 19 )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects al-Sakkākī's reading because a rhetor does not choose an individualizing indefinite when a better formulation is available.
rows.anchor: لأن المصير إلى الإفراد في القصد من التنكير مصير لا يختاره البليغ ما وجد عنه مندوحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “There is no god but He” explicitly reinforces oneness, preventing a reading of “one” as only unsurpassed in kind or as the Muslims' god alone.
rows.anchor: تأكيد لمعنى الوحدة وتنصيص عليها لرفع احتمال أن يكون المراد الكمال

rows.speaker: أبو سفيان
rows.claim: Abū Sufyān's taunt “We have al-ʿUzzā and you have no ʿUzzā” illustrates the polytheists' idea that Muslims had a distinct god.
rows.anchor: قول أبي سفيان : ( لنا العزى ولا عزى لكم )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause establishes monotheism by denying true divinity to everything besides God.
rows.anchor: وقد أفادت جملة { لا إلاه إلا هو } التوحيد لأنها نفت حقيقة الألوهية عن غير الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The predicate of lā is omitted and understood as “existing”; the author explains that this denies the gods currently claimed by polytheists, while their supposed eternality makes future proliferation irrelevant.
rows.anchor: فالتقدير لا إله موجود إلا هو . وقد عرضت حيرة للنحاة في تقدير الخبر

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī is said to hold that lā has no omitted predicate: the underlying order is “He is a god,” with ilāh moved before huwa for restriction by illā.
rows.anchor: ونسب إلى الزمخشري أنه لا تقدير لخبر هنا وأن أصل لا إلاه إلا هو هو إلاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr calls al-Zamakhsharī's analysis contrived; an inferred predicate merely clarifies meaning and is not equivalent to explicitly uttering “existing.”
rows.anchor: وهذا تكلف والحق عندي أن المقدرات لا مفاهيم لها فليس تقدير لا إلاه موجود بمنزلة النطق بقولك لا إلاه موجود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because lā negating an indefinite already negates the whole genus, “no god” means divinity is unrealized except for God.
rows.anchor: فإن لا النافية إذا نفت النكرة فقد دلت على نفي الجنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm describe the pronoun as the giver of great and subtle blessings; they praise God and hint at His unique divinity because others do not bestow blessings.
rows.anchor: وصفان للضمير ، أي المنعم بجلائل النعم ودقائقها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two names do not grammatically assert exclusivity, but in this argument they indirectly imply it; their pairing follows the discussion in al-Fātiḥa.
rows.anchor: وليس في الصفتين دلالة على الحصر ولكنهما تعريض به هنا لأن الكلام مسوق لإبطال ألوهية غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning al-Raḥmān aggravates the polytheists, who refused that name, as 25:60 recounts.
rows.anchor: على أن في ذكر صفة الرحمن إغاظة للمشركين فإنهم أبوا وصف الله بالرحمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Except He” is an exception from the negated genus of gods, leaving this individual alone; lā's predicate is commonly omitted when its negation already gives the intended meaning.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن قوله : { إلا هو } استثناء من الإلاه المنفي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A predicate is supplied when needed to limit the negation to a circumstance, as in “no man is in the house”; an exception or repetition can itself fill the apparent predicate slot.
rows.anchor: ولا تحتاج للخبر إلا إذا أريد تقييد النفي بحالة نحو لا رجل في الدار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr gives “no god but God” and “no lineage today and no friendship” as examples where the predicate is omitted, and calls Abū Ḥayyān's analysis strained.
rows.anchor: ألا ترى أنهم إذا وجدوا شيئا يسد مسد الخبر في الصورة حذفوا الخبر مع لا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rule for responding to an aggressor follows from sacred inviolability being answered in kind; calling the response “aggression” is lexical matching, as in 2:193.
rows.anchor: وقوله : { فمن اعتدى عليكم فاعتدوا عليه } تفريع عن قوله

rows.speaker: الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshāf calls this a concluding summary, a “fathfulah,” of the preceding argument.
rows.anchor: وهذا وجه قول ( الكشاف ) : إنه فذلكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the reciprocal response “aggression” is lexical matching, like the earlier phrasing “there is no aggression except against wrongdoers.”
rows.anchor: وسمي جزاء الاعتداء اعتداء مشاكلة على نحو ما تقدم آنفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “By the same measure” requires matching both degree and circumstances, including the sacred month or sacred territory.
rows.anchor: يشمل المماثلة في المقدار وفي الأحوال ككونه في الشهر الحرام أو البلد الحرام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fear God by keeping retaliation within its limits, since anger makes a person taking revenge prone to excess.
rows.anchor: أمر بالاتقاء في الاعتداء أي بألا يتجاوز الحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The imperative “know” signals the importance of what follows; divine company here is a metaphor for aid and protection, though it may also mean observing God's sacred limits outside necessity.
rows.anchor: فإن قولك في الخطاب : اعلم إنباء بأهمية ما سيلقى للمخاطب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spending command continues the command to fight in 2:190; because the enemy had superior resources, it calls all Muslims to fund preparation, not only combatants.
rows.anchor: هذه الجملة معطوفة على جملة { وقاتلوا في سبيل الله } ( البقرة : 190 ) الخ فإنهم لما أمروا بقتال عدوهم وكان العدو أوفر منهم عدة حرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command was needed because confidence in God and His promise could lead believers to stop short of full preparation; reliance on God's support does not cancel using known means of victory.
rows.anchor: تعهد الله لهم بالتأييد والنصر لا يسقط عنهم أخذ العدة المعروفة فلا يحسبوا أنهم غير مأمورين ببذل الوسع لوسائل النصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pursuing results without the means God established is an error and discourtesy toward the Creator of causes and outcomes, like the Israelites' refusal to fight in 5:24.
rows.anchor: فتطلب المسببات دون أسبابها غلط وسوء أدب مع خالق الأسباب ومسبباتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Muslims expend their full effort and do not neglect preparation, God supports what exceeds their capacity; He gave victory at Badr when they were few and had not fallen short.
rows.anchor: فالمسلمون إذا بذلوا وسعهم ، ولم يفرطوا في شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People who squander Muslim funds on desires, miss secure opportunities to prepare, and then demand victory are deluded; God may let their enemies prevail because of their neglect, while preserving the religion through subtle care.
rows.anchor: فأما أقوام يتلفون أموال المسلمين في شهواتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “God loves those who do good” concludes the exhortation to excellence: divine love is people's highest aim and leads to well-being in this life and the next; “the doers of good” means believers generally.
rows.anchor: وقوله : { إن الله يحب المحسنين } تذييل للترغيب في الإحسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse returns to the pilgrimage discussion and may attach to 2:189 across an intervening digression, or be linked to the prior sentence as one story following another.
rows.anchor: هذا عود إلى الكلام على العمرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse was revealed at al-Ḥudaybiya in year six, when the polytheists turned Muslims away from the House while they intended ʿumra, before Hajj was obligatory; Hajj is included to promise a future opportunity, a Qur'anic miracle.
rows.anchor: ولا خلاف في أن هذه الآية نزلت في الحديبية سنة ست

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ikmāl means completing what remains until the whole act is covered.
rows.anchor: والإتمام إكمال الشيء والإتيان على بقايا ما بقي منه حتى يستوعب جميعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Usually, an imperative to perform an act with a quality asks one already engaged in it to make it fully possess that quality; Ibn ʿĀshūr applies this to completing Hajj and cites fasting and treaty examples.
rows.anchor: أحدهما وهو الأكثر أن يكون المطلوب تحصيل وصف خاص للفعل المتعلق به الوصف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, a command for an act's quality can require beginning the act in that form from the outset, as with “that I may complete My favor upon you.”
rows.anchor: وثانيهما أن يجيء الأمر بوصف الفعل مرادا به تحصيل الفعل من أول وهلة على تلك الصفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This second usage is a direct command to produce two elements together, not metonymy or metaphor; the lexical event itself is usually the primary demand of an imperative.
rows.anchor: وهذا ضرب من ضروب التعبير ليس بكناية ولا مجاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording permits both readings: complete rites already begun without disruption or abandonment under enemy pressure, or perform them fully from the outset.
rows.anchor: والآية تحتمل الاستعمالين ، فإن كان الأول فهي أمر بإكمال الحج والعمرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers the first reading because it fits the preceding verses: complete the rites once begun and do not let hostility deter you.
rows.anchor: والمعنى الأول أظهر وأنسب بالآيات التي قبلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exhortation suggests that the central concern is undertaking Hajj for the first time, and also ʿumra on the view that it is obligatory.
rows.anchor: وكأن هذا التحريض مشير إلى أن المقصود الأهم من الحج والعمرة هنا هما الصرورة في الحج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite articles mark familiar kinds of worship: Hajj visits the Kaaba in a set season and includes standing at ʿArafa, while ʿumra has no set season and is performed individually.
rows.anchor: واللام في ( الحج والعمرة ) لتعريف الجنس

rows.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
rows.claim: In a report collected by al-Tirmidhī, the Prophet answered that ʿumra is not obligatory like Hajj, though performing it is better.
rows.anchor: ودليلنا حديث جابر بن عبد الله ، ( قيل : يا رسول الله العمرة واجبة مثل الحج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If ʿumra were obligatory the Prophet would have commanded it; weak compilations do not establish obligation.
rows.anchor: لأن عبادة مثل هذه لو كانت واجبة لأمر بها النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ولا يثبت وجوبها بتلفيقات ضعيفة

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reportedly said that, absent his scruple and having heard nothing from the Messenger, he would have declared ʿumra obligatory; Ibn ʿĀshūr relies on the latter clause.
rows.anchor: وقد روي عن ابن مسعود أنه كان يقول : لولا التحرج وأني لم أسمع من رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He argues that 3:97 obligates Hajj but not ʿumra, that two obligatory rites of the same type would not be imposed, and that an obligatory rite should have a fixed time.
rows.anchor: ولأن الله تعالى قال : { ولله على الناس حج البيت } ( آل عمران : 97 ) ولم يذكر العمرة

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: The author's school also cites the five-pillar report, Gabriel's report on faith and Islam, and the Bedouin who was told “he succeeds if truthful”; none mentions ʿumra.
rows.anchor: واحتج أصحابنا أيضا بحديث : ( بني الإسلام على خمس ) وحديث جبريل في الإيمان والإسلام

rows.speaker: الشافعية
rows.claim: The Shāfiʿīs rely on this verse pairing ʿumra with Hajj, reports from some Companions, and precaution to argue for its obligation.
rows.anchor: ولم يحتج الشافعية بأكثر من هذه الآية ، إذ قرنت فيها مع الحج

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: ʿUmar invoked “complete Hajj and ʿumra” to prohibit tamattuʿ: performing ʿumra and leaving ihram during the Hajj season before making Hajj that year and returning home.
rows.anchor: واحتج عمر بن الخطاب بهذه الآية على منع التمتع وهو الإحرام بعمرة ثم الحل منها في مدة الحج

rows.speaker: أبو موسى الأشعري
rows.claim: Abū Mūsā recounted that the Prophet sent him to Yemen; at the Farewell Pilgrimage he said he had entered ihram as the Prophet had, and the Prophet ordered him to circumambulate, walk between Ṣafā and Marwa, then exit ihram because he had no sacrificial animal.
rows.anchor: ففي البخاري أخرج حديث أبي موسى الأشعري قال : ( بعثني رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: أبو موسى الأشعري
rows.claim: Abū Mūsā said he followed this practice in his public rulings until ʿUmar's caliphate, when ʿUmar insisted on the Qur'anic command to complete Hajj and ʿumra and the Prophet's not exiting before the offering reached its destination.
rows.anchor: فكنت أفتي الناس به حتى خلافة عمر فذكرته له فقال : أن نأخذ بكتاب الله

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: ʿUmar reasoned that Abū Mūsā had entered ihram like the Prophet, who combined ʿumra and Hajj; a pilgrim in qirān is engaged in Hajj and cannot exit midway, as shown by the Prophet's own conduct.
rows.anchor: يريد عمر والله أعلم أن أبا موسى أهل بإهلال كإهلال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم والنبي كان مهلا بحجة وعمرة معا فهو قارن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿUmar's argument assumes an āḥād report cannot restrict a mass-transmitted rule, the same principle he applied to Fāṭima bt. Qays's maintenance report.
rows.anchor: وهذا مبني على عدم تخصيص المتواتر بالآحاد كما هو قوله في حديث فاطمة ابنة قيس في النفقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “if you are prevented” clause branches from the completion command and explains what to do when completion is blocked, especially for Hajj, whose time may expire before the obstacle lifts.
rows.anchor: وقوله : { فإن أحصرتم فما استيسر من الهدى } عطف على { أتموا }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iḥṣār in Arabic means an obstacle prevents someone from an act; the hamza in aḥṣara does not make it causative, and the verb is synonymous with ḥaṣara, as with ṣadda/aṣadda.
rows.anchor: والإحصار في كلام العرب منع الذات من فعل ما ، يقال

rows.speaker: المحققون من أئمة اللغة
rows.claim: Leading language authorities hold that aḥṣara is not causative and is synonymous with ḥaṣara; their usual applications differ, with aḥṣara for non-enemy obstruction and ḥaṣara for enemy obstruction.
rows.anchor: هذا قول المحققين من أئمة اللغة ، ولكن كثر استعمال أحصر المهموز

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the two verbs are literal for both senses, though usage tends to associate each with one type of obstacle.
rows.anchor: فهو حقيقة في المعنيين ولكن الاستعمال غلب أحدهما في أحدهما كما قال الزمخشري في ( الكشاف )

rows.speaker: الكسائي وأبو عبيدة والزجاج
rows.claim: These linguists distinguish the words categorically: aḥṣara is for obstruction other than an enemy, and ḥaṣara for an enemy.
rows.anchor: ومن اللغويين من قال : أحصر حقيقة في منع غير العدو وحصر حقيقة في منع العدو

rows.speaker: ابن فارس
rows.claim: Ibn Fāris reverses that distinction, a view Ibn ʿĀshūr calls highly anomalous.
rows.anchor: ومن اللغويين من عكس وهو ابن فارس لكنه شاذ جدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional uses in to present an unwelcome possibility as uncertain; it also signals that the polytheists would prevent Muslims from ʿumra.
rows.anchor: وجاء الشرط بحرف ( إن ) لأن مضمون الشرط كريه لهم فألقى إليهم الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers reading iḥṣār broadly for obstruction by an enemy or another cause, since “when you are secure” strongly implies release from fear of an enemy and the broad sense lets the concise passage combine the rulings then separate them.
rows.anchor: والأظهر عندي أن الإحصار هنا أطلق على ما يعم المنع من عدو أو من غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He suggests Mālik may have held the broad reading: in al-Muwaṭṭaʾ he based the rule for non-enemy obstruction on Sunnah rather than this verse.
rows.anchor: وكأن هذا هو الذي يراه مالك رحمه الله ، ولذلك لم يحتج في ( الموطأ ) على حكم الإحصار بغير عدو بهذه الآية

rows.speaker: جمهور أصحابه
rows.claim: Most Mālikī disciples say the verse concerns obstruction from illness or similar causes, not an enemy, following the more common lexical use and the verse's sacrificial requirement.
rows.anchor: وقال جمهور أصحابه أريد بها المنع الحاصل من مرض ونحوه دون منع العدو ، بناء على أن إطلاق الإحصار على هذا المنع هو الأكثر في اللغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Sunnah does not make an offering due merely to an enemy siege; someone who already brought an offering still performs that rite, but not because of the siege.
rows.anchor: ولأن هذه الآية جعلت على المحصر هديا ولم ترد السنة بمشروعية الهدي فيمن حصره العدو

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Mālik requires an offering for obstruction by illness, postpartum bleeding, fracture, or another impediment to standing with the pilgrims, followed by ṭawāf and saʿy when it lifts and a make-up Hajj the next year.
rows.anchor: ولذلك قال مالك بوجوب الهدي على من أحصر بمرض أو نفاس أو كسر

rows.speaker: معْبد بن حزابة المخزومي
rows.claim: In al-Muwaṭṭaʾ, Maʿbad b. Ḥazāba fell on the road to Mecca while in ihram; Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn al-Zubayr, and Marwān told him to treat himself and sacrifice, then make ʿumra after recovery and Hajj the following year.
rows.anchor: لما في ( الموطأ ) من حديث معبد بن حزابة المخزومي أنه صرع ببعض طريق مكة وهو محرم

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: ʿUmar gave the same instruction to Abū Ayyūb and Habbār b. al-Aswad when they missed the standing at ʿArafa.
rows.anchor: وأن عمر بن الخطاب أمر بذلك أبا أيوب وهبار بن الأسود حين فاتهما وقوف عرفة

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Mālik argued that the Prophet did not order companions blocked by enemy siege either to make up a rite or return for another one.
rows.anchor: واحتج في ( الموطأ ) بأن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم لم يأمر أحدا من أصحابه ولا من كان معه

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: The author's school distinguishes illness, an impediment intrinsic to the pilgrim, which still obliges completion, from an enemy blockade, an external impediment.
rows.anchor: ووجه أصحابنا ذلك بالتفرقة ؛ لأن المانع في المرض ونحوه من ذات الحاج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the verse can cover either type of obstruction, Ibn ʿĀshūr says illness or another non-enemy obstruction is more apparent, and the Sunnah reinforces that reading.
rows.anchor: والأظهر في الاستدلال أن الآية وإن صلحت لكل منع لكنها في منع غير العدو أظهر
